name: Lipstick effect

lead: The lipstick effect is the idea that when the economy weakens, consumers cut big discretionary purchases but still spend on small, affordable luxuries such as lipstick. In appearance terms it describes why makeup and grooming remain in demand when budgets tighten: they are a cheap way to look better.

Researchers have tested it. A 2012 set of studies found that recession cues raised women's desire for attractiveness-enhancing products, and a 2016 study found economic worry also pushed women toward improving their professional appearance. Whether lipstick sales actually rise in real recessions has been disputed, with mixed data.

paras: In practice the effect shows up as people choosing low-cost cosmetics, nail polish, fragrance or grooming items as a lower-priced way to polish their appearance. It is an economic and psychological observation, not a routine.

There is no health risk in the concept itself. One 2022 dermatology report during COVID-19 lockdowns described complications from unsupervised home cosmetic procedures bought online, which the authors linked to misinformation and unregulated products rather than to lipstick.

angle.text: The lipstick effect is an explanation for why people turn to low-cost cosmetics to improve their look under financial pressure. Studies connect this to wanting to appear more attractive to partners and to look more professional.

lead: The lipstick effect is the hypothesis that consumers keep buying inexpensive luxuries such as lipstick during downturns even as they cut larger discretionary spending. The related 'lipstick index' proposes lipstick sales as an economic indicator. Leonard Lauder, chairman of Estée Lauder, popularised the idea in 2001, and a Wall Street Journal report that year noted an 11% rise in US mass-market lipstick sales in the months after the September 11 attacks.[1]

For appearance, the effect describes why affordable cosmetics stay in demand when money is tight: small products offer a visible improvement in how someone looks. Psychology research has proposed that the motive is attracting resource-secure partners, and later that it also includes making a better impression at work.[2][3]

Historical sales data are inconsistent. Commentary cited by Wikipedia notes mixed figures for the Great Depression and the 2007-2009 recession, and a 2020 study found lipstick's income elasticity fell during 2007-2009 rather than showing a clear rise.[1]
infobox: Hill et al., 2012; Netchaeva and Rouen, 2016

paras: Leonard Lauder popularised the term in 2001, suggesting lipstick sales rise as the economy weakens because shoppers trade big purchases for small ones.[1] Economist Juliet Schor had earlier discussed prestige lipstick brands as conspicuous consumption in 1998.[1]

A 2012 paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology reported that recession cues, whether natural or experimentally primed, lowered desire for most products but increased women's desire for products that raise attractiveness to mates; the effect was driven by wanting to attract partners with resources.[2]

A 2016 Psychological Science study proposed that heightened economic concern also increased women's desire to use appearance-enhancing items to make a favourable impression in the workplace, and found women with high economic concern chose to improve professional appearance more often than romantic attractiveness.[3]

The effect is debated as an economic indicator. Reported lipstick sales in the Great Recession fell by 5.8% in 2008 by one account, and a 2009 Economist analysis found no clear inverse link with economic conditions.[1] A 2020 study of US scanner data found lipstick income elasticity dropped from about 0.31 to 0.05 in 2007-2009.[1]

During COVID-19, mask wearing shifted demand: reported Japanese lipstick sales for January to October 2020 fell to 44% of 2019 levels, while eye makeup fell to 88%.[1] A Korean survey of 600 consumers in 2020-2021 reported that usability and price positively shaped attitudes to lip products.[4]

Commentators have proposed a nail polish index; a 2011 Reuters report cited a 42% rise in French department-store nail polish sales in 2010.[1] A 2022 Clinics in Dermatology report that used the term described complications in patients who bought injectables and peel products online for home use during lockdown.[5]
No studies found. Behavioural experiments are described above.[2][3]
